openers.fert: A plant cannot live on sunlight and water alone. It needs nutrients, the substances an organism uses to survive, grow and reproduce, and sixteen chemical elements are usually listed as essential for its growth and reproduction. This part of the course follows how soil supplies them, and what happens when it stops. History offers hard lessons, from the burned and overgrazed fields of colonial New England to the worn-out land of Southern slave plantations. It also shows how laboratory analysis and careful planning try to match each field's supply to each crop's needs.
openers.nutrients-and-plant-nutrition: Growth is set not by the total resources a plant has but by the scarcest one. That simple principle runs through this chapter. It begins with the substances an organism uses to survive, grow and reproduce, and with the sixteen elements a plant must have to complete its life cycle. It then asks what lets a soil sustain steady, high-quality yields, how that ability declines when what a soil gives is never replaced, and how a laboratory analysis of a soil sample can show what a field lacks.

soil-fert-181.title: Nutrients, the raw materials of every living thing
soil-fert-181.text: The minerals on a dinner plate began in the soil. Plants take their minerals from the soil, so the minerals in the human diet come from plants eaten directly or from animals that ate them. A nutrient is any substance an organism uses to survive, grow and reproduce. Animals, plants, fungi and protists all need nutrients, though different kinds of organism have different essential ones. Some nutrients are organic, such as proteins, fats, sugars and vitamins. Others are inorganic, such as iron, selenium and zinc. An essential nutrient is one an organism needs for normal function but cannot make itself, at all or in sufficient amounts. Plants absorb a wide range of minerals through their roots and take in carbon dioxide and oxygen through their leaves. Too little of a nutrient is a deficiency. Harm from too much is nutrient toxicity.

soil-fert-149.title: Soil fertility: what lets a field feed a crop year after year
soil-fert-149.text: A fertile soil does far more than hold a plant upright. Soil fertility is the ability of a soil to sustain agricultural plant growth, giving plants a habitat and steady, high-quality yields. Such a soil supplies essential nutrients and water in adequate amounts and proportions. It is also free of toxic substances, such as Fe2+, that inhibit growth. Several properties add up to fertility. A fertile soil is deep enough for roots and stored water, drains and breathes well inside, and has an organic-rich topsoil. Its nutrients are in plant-available forms, and its microorganisms support plant growth. A soil pH between 5.5 and 7.0 suits most plants, though some prefer or tolerate more acid or alkaline conditions. Beneath all this runs constant cycling. Microbes decomposing plant and animal wastes release inorganic nutrients, while microbes competing with plants tie them up again. Negatively charged clay and humus hold nutrient cations, such as potassium and many trace elements, by cation exchange, which strongly influences fertility. Growing crops does not by itself exhaust a soil, as long as mineral weathering replaces the nutrients carried off in harvests. Improper irrigation and acid rain can still deplete it. On farmed land, keeping fertility usually requires conserving the soil itself, because erosion and other degradation lower soil quality. History shows the cost of neglect. Colonial land practices, slavery, and the rise of intensive farming and forestry have all damaged soil fertility and quality.

soil-fert-156.title: Plant nutrition: what a plant feeds on, and how
soil-fert-156.text: For most of history, nobody knew what plants actually fed on. Aristotle and later investigators puzzled over what plant nutrients were and how plants absorbed and transported them. Plant nutrition is the study of the chemical elements and compounds plants need for growth, reproduction and metabolism, and of how they are supplied. An element counts as essential if a plant cannot complete a normal life cycle without it. It also counts if it is part of an essential plant constituent or metabolite. {{ref:soil-hist-004}} proved in 1840 that plants need nitrogen, potassium and phosphorus. In 1939 Arnon and Stout grew plants without soil to show that molybdenum is essential to tomatoes. Plants take carbon, hydrogen and oxygen from air and water. Most other nutrients, nitrogen included, come from the soil. There the elements sit as salts, so plants absorb them as ions, atoms or small molecules carrying an electric charge. Amount alone is not enough. Nutrients must arrive in suitable ratios, and needs vary between species and even between individuals of one clone. Most soils can fully nourish the plants adapted to them. Cropped soil is different. It needs {{ref:soil-fert-001}} to sustain yields, because a nutrient deficiency limits growth even when water and light are ample.

soil-fert-151.title: Soil depletion: spending the soil's nutrient bank
soil-fert-151.text: Topsoil takes hundreds to thousands of years to form, and it can be spent far faster. Soil depletion is the decline of a soil's fertility when what makes it fertile is removed and not replaced. The conditions that support fertility are not maintained either. It leads to poor harvests and is becoming a global problem. On farms it stems from overly intensive cultivation and careless handling of the land. Over-tillage, salinization and overuse of nutrient inputs all contribute, the last of these mining the soil's nutrient bank. Rapid changes in land use can also severely challenge soil fertility. As of 2008, depletion was among the most widespread problems in tropical zones, where soils are low in nutrients. In the Middle East, drought, erosion and lack of irrigation hamper farming, and productivity has fallen most steeply in hilly and dryland areas. Across much of Africa fertile soil is being depleted, notably in the Sahel under high population pressure. Farmers there use artificial and natural fertilizers to restore nutrients. The stakes can be enormous. Topsoil depletion, the erosion or exhaustion of organic topsoil, has been blamed for the collapse of many past civilizations.

soil-fert-169.title: Sixteen elements every plant must have
soil-fert-169.text: A plant's whole life rests on a short list of chemical elements. The essential plant nutrients are the elements a plant must have to complete its life cycle, and sixteen are usually listed. They are carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, sulfur, calcium, magnesium, iron, boron, manganese, copper, zinc, molybdenum and chlorine. Some sources add nickel, for seventeen. Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen come from carbon dioxide and water. Nitrogen comes from {{ref:soil-fert-100}}. Every other element comes originally from the soil's mineral fraction. Plants can take up a nutrient only in a plant-available form, mostly as ions absorbed from the soil water. That is the catch. Most nutrients are locked in primary and secondary minerals that weather too slowly for rapid growth. Even ground feldspar or apatite seldom supplies enough potassium or phosphorus. A more accessible reservoir sits on clay colloids and organic matter, which hold nutrients exchangeably and refill the soil solution as plants draw it down. Microbial decomposition of organic matter refills it too, which matters most for nitrogen, sulfur, phosphorus and boron. Gram for gram, humus holds far more nutrients and water than clay minerals, and it supplies most of a soil's cation exchange capacity. Balance counts as well. Under {{ref:soil-fert-182}}, a nutrient short in the soil solution keeps others from being taken up at the best rate, so optimal growth needs a particular nutrient ratio.

soil-fert-187.title: Soil tests: asking a field what it lacks
soil-fert-187.text: Before adding fertilizer, a grower can ask the soil what it needs. A soil test is a laboratory or in-situ analysis of a soil's chemical, physical or biological characteristics. The most widely run tests estimate plant-available nutrient concentrations to guide fertilizer recommendations. It reveals deficiencies and possible toxicities, and it is meant to mimic how roots take up minerals. Sampling matters. Labs such as Iowa State and Colorado State recommend 10–20 sample points per 40 acres, and composite sampling mixes soil from several spots. Nutrients vary with depth and time, so samples are best analyzed within about 24 hours, or else frozen or air-dried. Methods differ widely. Europe alone uses more than 10 tests for plant-available phosphorus, and their results are not directly comparable. Some labs analyze all 13 mineral nutrients plus a dozen potentially toxic elements with one 'universal soil extractant', ammonium bicarbonate DTPA. Do-it-yourself kits usually test only N, P, K and pH and are less accurate.

soil-fert-152.title: How colonial New England wore out its soil
soil-fert-152.text: Colonists in New England let their herd animals roam and did not return the animals' dung to the soil. Settlers unfamiliar with Indigenous farming also burned land intensively and turned cattle loose to save labor, ruining fertility and preventing sustainable cropping. Historian William Cronon blamed the erosion that followed on forest removal, more destructive floods, compaction and close-cropping by grazing animals, and plowing. The damage did not stay in New England. About one-half of the Great Plains' original topsoil has disappeared since farming began there in the 1880s, as {{ref:soil-water-075}} showed.

soil-fert-155.title: When irrigation water helps or harms a soil
soil-fert-155.text: About 18% of the world's cropland is irrigated today, and the water's chemistry shapes every soil it soaks. Highly alkaline water builds up sodium salts that ruin drainage, so roots cannot penetrate deeply into the resulting alkali soils. Acidic water drains away useful Ca, Mg, K, P and S, and dissolves aluminum and manganese salts that impede growth. Saline water, or poor drainage of irrigated land, turns soil saline and infertile. Saline water also hinders roots' uptake of water and nutrients. Handled well or badly, irrigation can maintain, degrade or improve a soil's fertility and tilth.

soil-fert-153.title: Worn-out land on the slave plantations of the South
soil-fert-153.text: Southern plantation owners sought to maximize the labor they extracted, not the output of each acre. Historian David Silkenat explains that they treated the landscape as disposable and enslaved Africans as expendable. After forcing enslaved people to clear forests, planters abandoned the worn land and moved on to more fertile ground. Swamps were drained, forests cleared to grow single crops and to fuel steamships, and invasive species introduced. The results were eroded hillsides, rivers clogged with sterile soil, and extinct native species.

soil-fert-154.title: Albert Howard's case: health begins in the soil
soil-fert-154.text: In 1945 Albert Howard wrote that all future studies of disease must begin with the soil. He called soil fertility the basis of the public health system of the future. His idea was that the health of crops, livestock and people starts with a fertile, well-kept soil. Howard is credited as the first Westerner to publish Native techniques of sustainable agriculture. He argued that industrial agriculture upsets the balance of nature and irrevocably robs the soil of its fertility.

soil-fert-192.title: Nutrient management: right source, rate, time and place
soil-fert-192.text: Using less nitrogen fertilizer could avoid nitrous oxide emissions equal to 2.77–11.48 gigatons of carbon dioxide from 2020 to 2050. That saving is one prize of nutrient management. It links soil, crop, weather and water conditions with farming and conservation practices. The goal is to use nutrients efficiently for yield, quality and profit while losing little to the environment. It matches the rate, source, timing and placement of nutrients to each field's soil, climate and crop, an approach known as 4R nutrient stewardship. The International Plant Nutrition Institute's 4R manual sets out the right source, rate, time and place. Managers plan applications for achievable yields and budget all nutrient sources and sinks at the site. They manage soil, water and crop to curb leaching, runoff and volatilization, the escape of nutrients as gas. The pathways interact. A practice that cuts runoff of one nutrient may increase leaching of others.

soil-fert-182.title: Liebig's law: the scarcest nutrient sets the limit
soil-fert-182.text: Farmers who added more of a plentiful nutrient saw no gain in growth, while adding the scarce one worked. Explaining that puzzle gave agriculture one of its best-known rules. Liebig's law of the minimum holds that growth is set not by the total resources available but by the scarcest one, the limiting factor. Carl Sprengel developed it in agricultural science in 1840, and the chemist Liebig later popularized it. In soil terms, when one nutrient is short in the soil solution, stoichiometry keeps the plant from taking up the others at an optimal rate. Stoichiometry means the fixed proportions in which elements are combined. The law spread well beyond the farm. It has been extended to biological populations, and ecosystem models commonly use it for factors such as sunlight, nitrate or phosphate. In the sea, phytoplankton can be limited by iron in nutrient-rich coastal upwellings and by nitrogen and phosphorus in the nutrient-poor open ocean. In natural resource management it implies that growth is restricted by the scarcest input. Phosphorus has no substitute, so it will have to be recycled. The law is not the last word, though. Diagnosing limiting factors is still a common study, but the approach has been criticized. In plant nutrition, models that allow for interactions between nutrients have replaced it.

soil-fert-158.title: Macronutrients and micronutrients: sorting by appetite
soil-fert-158.text: The labels describe a plant's appetite, not the soil's pantry. Macronutrients are taken up in relatively large amounts, and micronutrients are needed only in small amounts. Neither term says how abundant an element is in the soil. The soil supplies the macronutrients nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulfur in relatively large amounts. Four elements dominate a plant's body: hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and carbon together make up over 95% of its dry biomass. The micronutrients are iron, boron, chlorine, manganese, zinc, copper, molybdenum and nickel. They occur in plant tissue at 0.1 to 200 ppm, or parts per million, under 0.02% of dry weight. Soil laboratories use a three-way split instead. Major nutrients are N, P and K. Secondary ones are S, Ca and Mg. Minor ones are Fe, Mn, Cu, Zn, B, Mo and Cl. Beyond plants, carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur are the elemental macronutrients of all organisms.

soil-fert-150.title: Fertilizing soil: topping up phosphorus, nitrogen and potassium
soil-fert-150.text: Soil fertilization adds the nutrients a soil most often lacks for crops: phosphorus, nitrogen and potassium, the three elements every commercial fertilizer analysis lists. Bioavailable phosphorus is the element most often lacking, especially in humid tropical soils. Inorganic fertilizers need less labor and carry more concentrated nutrients than organic ones. Plants take up N, P and K in inorganic forms, so these fertilizers act at once. Relying on them too heavily upsets the soil's nutrient balance. Soil quality and organic matter fall, erosion risk rises, and soluble nitrate pollutes water. Slow-release fertilizers can cut leaching and spread the supply over a longer period.

soil-fert-179.title: Micronutrients: tiny doses that run every enzyme
soil-fert-179.text: Every process that supports plant growth runs through a protein containing a micronutrient. Plant micronutrients are essential elements needed only in very small amounts, mostly as required parts of enzyme systems. In order of importance they include chlorine, iron, manganese, boron, zinc, copper and molybdenum. Manganese builds the structure of photosystem II and helps build chloroplasts. Copper aids photosynthesis and the forming of lignin, and chlorine serves osmosis and ionic balance. Nickel activates urease, the enzyme that processes {{ref:soil-fert-021}}; without nickel, this nitrogen compound builds up to toxic levels and causes necrotic lesions. Molybdenum is part of nitrate reductase and of {{ref:soil-fert-101}}, the enzyme bacteria use to fix nitrogen. Soil minerals generally supply enough, but heavy phosphate use can cause zinc and iron deficiency by forming insoluble phosphates. Too little uptake causes deficiencies, such as chlorosis, a yellowing of leaves, from a lack of copper, iron, manganese or zinc. Too much causes toxicity. Some micronutrients can be applied as seed coatings, and acidifying fertilizers that supply nitrogen keep their cations soluble longer in alkaline soils.

soil-fert-162.title: Where symptoms show: nutrients that move and nutrients that stay
soil-fert-162.text: Where a leaf yellows on a plant is a clue to what the plant lacks. Nutrient mobility is how readily a nutrient can be moved within a plant from older tissues to where it is most needed. Plants send nutrients preferentially to their younger leaves. Nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and magnesium are mobile, so their deficiencies show first on the oldest leaves. Nitrogen moves in the xylem, the water-carrying tissue, as nitrate or organic compounds. In the phloem, the sap-carrying tissue, it moves as amides, amino acids and ureides. Calcium is immobile in the phloem and arrives only with transpiration through the xylem, so its deficiency shows in new growth. Boron and sulfur cannot be remobilized from older leaves either, so their deficiencies appear first in the youngest tissues. Where symptoms appear therefore helps diagnose which nutrient a plant lacks.

soil-fert-163.title: Reading a hungry plant: signs of nutrient deficiency
soil-fert-163.text: Crops can starve without looking starved. Nutrient deficiency covers the effects of too little of an essential nutrient, from slightly slower growth to stunting, deformity, discoloration and death. Clear-cut symptoms are rare, because most deficiencies are multiple and moderate. Nitrogen is most often the nutrient in shortest supply. Its lack brings stunted, slow growth and chlorosis, sometimes with purple stems and leaf undersides from the pigment anthocyanin. Phosphorus deficiency is hard to diagnose, though leaves may turn intensely green, reddish or purple. Calcium deficiency weakens root systems and causes blossom end rot in tomatoes, peppers and watermelons, bitter pit in apples and black heart in celery. Potassium deficiency starts in older tissues, with necrosis or interveinal chlorosis, wilting, more disease and greater frost and heat damage. Iron, manganese and copper deficiencies show on new growth, molybdenum on older growth, zinc on old and new leaves, and boron on terminal buds. Chlorosis is not always about nutrients. Solarization looks similar, but unlike deficiency it causes no early leaf drop.

soil-fert-197.title: Molybdenum deficiency and the whiptail cauliflower
soil-fert-197.text: In cauliflower and other Brassica crops, molybdenum deficiency shows up as whiptail. It arises from soils low in molybdenum, or from strong sorption that holds it unavailable. Sorption is strongest in acid soils, so acid sandy soils suffer most. Plants need molybdenum for nitrate reductase, xanthine dehydrogenase and the nitrogen-fixing enzyme. Deficient plants therefore accumulate nitrate, and legumes fix less nitrogen. Leaves turn pale and scalded. Leaf contents of 0.2–2.0 mg/kg suffice for most crops. Adding lime often helps by reducing sorption, but molybdenum fertilizer such as sodium molybdate is often far more cost-effective.

soil-fert-172.title: Nitrogen, the nutrient plants want most
soil-fert-172.text: Plants are bathed in nitrogen yet often starve for it. Air is nearly 79% N2, but the triple bond in that molecule makes it almost inert. It must be fixed as ammonium or nitrate before plants can use it. Nitrogen is the most critical nutrient plants take from soil and often limits growth, except in tropical rainforests, where phosphorus limits instead. Its compounds make up 40% to 50% of the dry matter of protoplasm. Most soil nitrogen is bound in organic matter and must be mineralized, released as ammonium or nitrate. Mycorrhizal fungi give plants access to some organic nitrogen. Net mineralization adds about 50 kg per hectare on average, the main usable source in unfertilized fields. Bacteria in legume root nodules may add 200 to 300 kg per hectare per year, possibly enough for the crop. Cultivation lowers soil nitrogen, and no-till soils keep more than tilled ones. Plants take up most nitrogen as nitrate, but ammonium dominates in acid environments such as boreal forests, where the microbial conversion of ammonium to nitrate is less likely.

soil-fert-184.title: The carbon-to-nitrogen ratio: a microbe's diet in one number
soil-fert-184.text: Dig sawdust into a garden and the plants may go short of nitrogen. The carbon-to-nitrogen ratio compares the mass of carbon with the mass of nitrogen in organic residues. In soil it expresses the balance between energy food for microbes, the carbon, and protein-building material, the nitrogen. Plant residues typically run from 13:1 to 100:1, from alfalfa at 13 to oat straw at 80. Sawdust reaches 250, while bacteria are only 4. Above 30:1, microbes run short of nitrogen and take up soil ammonium and nitrate, locking them away. Plants then compete with microbes for nitrogen until the microbes die. Below 15, mineral nitrogen is freed for plants, though excess nitrogen may be leached. A ratio around 24:1 gives high microbial activity, 30:1 is recommended for soil materials, and microbes themselves are about 10:1. As microbes and soil fauna digest organic matter and release CO2, the ratio falls. A lower soil ratio correlates with higher productivity. Added organic materials can shift a soil's ratio, and a soil test can measure it.

soil-fert-170.title: How nutrients travel the last few millimeters to a root
soil-fert-170.text: A root quickly empties the soil it touches. Nutrients in contact with a root are used up within about 2 mm, so most ions must travel some distance through the soil solution. Three routes bring them. In mass flow, dissolved nutrients ride with the water moving toward a transpiring root, like leaves floating down a stream. In diffusion, ions move by random motion from richer soil toward the depleted zone at the root surface. Diffusion keeps going even when closed stomata, the pores of leaves, halt mass flow. Root interception, the slowest route, works as roots grow into new, undepleted soil. The routes split the work unevenly. For corn, mass flow is estimated to supply 98.8% of nitrogen and 95.0% of sulfur. Diffusion supplies 90.9% of phosphorus and 77.7% of potassium. Roots absorb these two so fast that their concentration next to the root falls almost to zero, which drives the diffusion. Decomposing organic matter holds 90–95% of soil nitrogen and sulfur and 20–75% of soil phosphorus, so it supplies much of plants' anion nutrients. Where crops are grown, this natural replenishment of the soil solution usually has to be topped up with fertilizer or organic matter.

soil-fert-157.title: Root uptake: how ions cross into a plant
soil-fert-157.text: Roots do not simply soak up nutrients; they trade for them. Root hairs pump hydrogen ions into the soil. These displace cations held on negatively charged soil particles, freeing them for uptake. Root nutrient uptake is how plants take essential elements in through their roots, above all the root hairs, and pass them to the conducting tissues. In the root apoplast, the spaces in and between cell walls, H+ is exchanged for other cations, and bicarbonate and hydroxide for nutrient anions. Ions then travel to the stele, the root's central core, to reach the xylem and phloem. On the way, the Casparian strip blocks passive flow and so regulates what enters. Uptake works three ways. Nonpolar molecules cross by simple diffusion, others by facilitated diffusion through transport proteins, and still others by active transport against a concentration gradient, using ATP-powered pumps. Because uptake is an active metabolic process, waterlogging, compaction, extreme soil temperatures and poor sugar supply to roots can all inhibit it. The root's structure and architecture can change the rate too. Partners help. Nitrogen-fixing rhizobia and mycorrhizal fungi, which enlarge the effective root surface, both enhance nutrient uptake.

soil-fert-174.title: Phosphorus: the energy element that stays put
soil-fert-174.text: The world may already have passed its peak of phosphorus. Rock phosphate reserves are limited and being depleted by fertilizer use. The peak in phosphorus output, {{ref:soil-fert-046}}, is estimated to have come in 1988 for the U.S. and 1989 for the world. After nitrogen, phosphorus is probably the element most likely to be deficient in soils. In plants it forms DNA, RNA and membrane phospholipids, and as part of ATP it underpins every energy transfer in the cell. Total soil phosphorus averages 0.06 percent by weight, mostly in organic forms that stay unavailable until mineralized or passed to plants by arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi. Dissolved phosphate not quickly taken up forms insoluble calcium phosphates or ends up with iron and aluminum hydrous oxides. In tropical soils, leaching and weathering have depleted it, and unlike nitrogen it cannot be replenished from the air. Phosphorus is largely immobile in soil. It builds up in the surface layer if not cropped and reaches roots mainly by diffusion. It is most available at pH 6.5 in mineral soils and 5.5 in organic soils. On some soils, spruces and other conifers depend on mycorrhizae for it.

soil-fert-175.title: Potassium, the gatekeeper of a leaf's pores
soil-fert-175.text: Potassium opens and closes a leaf's stomata through an ion pump. It therefore controls water loss from leaves and raises drought tolerance. This primary nutrient is present in all plant parts and activates enzymes of photosynthesis and respiration, yet it is built into no major plant constituent. In plant tissue it is outstandingly mobile and soluble. Soils hold 3 to 100 tons of potassium per hectare in the top 20 cm, but only 2 per cent of it is available to plants. Biotite mica and potassium feldspar are common mineral sources, and rhizobacteria help dissolve it with organic acids. Once dissolved, about half is held as exchangeable cations on clay minerals and half stays in the soil solution. As soils dry, potassium can be fixed between the layers of 2:1 clays such as illite, vermiculite and montmorillonite, up to 90 percent within ten minutes. It leaches easily from low-clay soils unless dressings of animal dung or lime offset their poor cation exchange capacity. Potassium-rich soils also yield quality fruit, with better color, shape and sugar content.

soil-fert-189.title: Soil tests for engineers
soil-fert-189.text: Engineers test soil for different reasons than farmers do. In geotechnical engineering, soil tests measure physical characteristics such as water content, void ratio and bulk density. They also give information on shear strength, rate of consolidation and permeability. Grain size analysis, by sieve or hydrometer, is one example. Constant-head and falling-head permeability tests are others.

soil-fert-188.title: Grid sampling: mapping a field's nutrients square by square
soil-fert-188.text: Nutrients are rarely spread evenly across a field. Grid soil sampling collects GPS-located samples on a regular grid to estimate how they vary. The distribution and resolution of the samples are chosen to capture the field's spatial variability, weighing the goals of the analysis against the cost of sampling. In U.S. corn and soybean regions, many providers offer one sample per 2.5-acre grid. A reference map recording sample locations and quantities is needed to interpret the results.
